Text: HI:    Okay; good morning.

HI:    This is Brittany Hibbert with the Samuel Proctor      Oral History Program from the University of Florida; and I am      currently in Sunflower; Mississippi; with Breyanna Hooper on September      21; 2013.
HI:    We will be talking about her involvement with the Sunflower      County Freedom Project.
HI:    So good morning; Breyanna.
HI:    Thank you for doing      this interview.
HI:    I want to go ahead and start with; if you could state      your name and then spell it for us—both names.
HO:    Okay.
HO:    My name is Breyanna Hooper.
HO:    Its spelled B-R-E-Y-A-N-N-A H-O-O-P-      E-R
HI:    Okay.
HI:    So; first of all; how old are you?
HO:    I am fifteen.
HI:    You’re fifteen.
HI:    And have you been in Sunflower County your whole      life?
HO:    I have not.
HO:    I am originally from Tallahatchie County.
HI:    Okay; so is it a big difference; as far as what you experienced being      a young woman in that county and being here in Sunflower?
HO:    Not at all.
HO:    The difference is the violence:
HO:    it’s more violent here      than it was there.
HI:    When you say violence; what type of violence are you talking about?
HO:    It’s been a lot of killing; that type of...
HO:    murder.
HO:    It’s like      drugs; things of that sort.
HI:    Do you feel safe here; or do you feel safer in the other county?
HO:    Actually; I feel safer in Tallahatchie.
HO:    Not because that’s where I’m      originally from; but in Tallahatchie; I stay in the country.
HO:    So; it’s      like nothing out there; but like Elmwood and a lot of trees and stuff.
HI:    Now as a young woman; what are you most afraid of about being here in      Sunflower County?
HO:    The gang violence.
HO:    It’s like so out of control; it’s even in school;      just out of control it is.
HO:    Like last year; our school was on lockdown      so many times because of the violence.
HI:    Okay.
HI:    Do you feel like your school is a safe place for you?
HI:    Like;      what school do you go to?
HO:    I attend Ruleville Central High School; and it is not a safe place at      all.
HI:    And what grade are you in?
HO:    I’m a sophomore.
HI:    I guess; what does the Sunflower County Freedom Project School mean      for you—you being able to come here and have somewhere to go?
HO:    So; in Drew—that’s where I stay now; in Drew; Mississippi—it’s not      like a lot of opportunities for anyone.
HO:    Not just people my age; but      anyone—not even the adults.

HO:    And I didn’t know about the Freedom      Project until I was; like; eighth grade; and when I heard about it; I      was like; this is what I have to do; because I just felt like; it can      get me to where I want to be in life.
HO:    I think it’s a really good      organization.
HI:    And what to do you want to be?
HO:    I want to be a psychologist.
HI:    Really?
HO:    Yes.
HI:    So what; have you looked into any colleges; and where are you      thinking about going?
HO:    I want to attend Spelman College.
HI:    In Atlanta; Georgia.
HO:    Yes.
HI:    All right; are you excited about getting ready to start applying for      college and stuff like that?
HO:    I am very excited.
HO:    I was looking online; like; a few weeks ago; and      I’m trying to get a trip to Spelman; to stay for like a weekend to see      if I would like the college atmosphere.
HI:    Mm-hm.
HI:    How often do you come to the Sunflower County Freedom Project;      and how far is it from Drew?
HO:    Maybe a thirty-minute drive; but that’s only because we have to pick      up students in between.
HO:    And I come Monday through Thursdays and then      on Saturdays.
HI:    Okay; so do you come after school; or in the morning?
HO:    After school.
HO:    It’s like an after school program; so it’s from 5:
HO:    0 to      7:
HO:    0 every day.
HO:    Except for on Saturdays:
HO:    it’s from 9:
HO:    0 to 2:
HO:    0.
HI:    And how would you describe your teachers here?
HO:    They are—I’ll use special; like I don’t this way to say what they      are—
HI:    Well; you can speak honestly.
HI:    Speak honestly.
HO:    Okay; they are special.
HO:    They’re; like; different.
HO:    Our teachers in      school; they help us; but here they help us in a special kind of way;      like; they go far and beyond to get what we need.
HO:    But in school; our      teachers are like; okay; this is what you have; and you have it.
HO:    But      they like; they teach us what we need to know; but they teach us      things past it; and I like that.
HI:    So; who would be your favorite teacher here; and why?
HO:    Missus Lumnah would have to be my favorite teacher here.
HI:    Missus who?
HO:    Missus Lumnah.
HI:    Lumnah?
HI:    Can you spell her name?
HO:    L-U-M-N-A-H
HI:    Okay; and why is she your favorite teacher?
HO:    She explains stuff; like; really good.
HO:    And her voice; or the tone      that she uses; a lot of people would think that she’s explaining stuff      to them to make them seem slow; like you know; kind of remedial.
HO:    But      she does this so that you will understand; and I like that.
HI:    Okay; and what kind of work do you guys normally do here?
HO:    It depends on the day.
HO:    So; we have different activities.
HO:    Like on      Thursdays; our club night; we have yoga; hip hop; drama.
HO:    And in      the—well; not the morning; but at the beginning before club; every day      before we do any extracurricular activity; we have a study session.
HO:    At      the Freedom Project; getting your homework done is the main priority;      so that’s what we get done first.
HO:    Then; at the later part of the day;      that’s when we do the different activities.
HI:    What do they usually prepare you guys for here?
HI:    So; are you doing      only school work; or are they helping you with; like; preparing for      college; studying for the SAT or ACT?
HI:    Are they helping you learn how      to figure out the FAFSA; or are they helping you apply for college?
HI:         What kind of help do you guys get here?
HO:    We get all the help we need; like honestly; it’s help for everything.
HO:         Like this class over here; is the college-prep class.
HO:    And; as you can      see; it’s the college research board right there:
HO:    only seniors take      this class; though; ‘cause you know; they’re getting ready for      college.
HO:    They do help you apply for college.
HO:    They get you into      special—well; not special; but they get you into summer opportunities;      like some of the students here did the Winters Institute Program at      Ole Miss.
HO:    And Mckayla Clayton; she is like a senior that just      graduated; and she’s; like; not part of the Project anymore; but she      goes to Elon University in North Carolina.
HI:    Okay.
HI:    So do you feel prepared for college?
HI:    Like; I know you’re only a      sophomore; but do you feel like you’re prepared already for what could      be coming?
HO:    I do.
HI:    Okay.
HI:    So; I know that you previously said that you’re a sophomore.
HI:         But do you honestly feel as though you’re already prepared being here      at the Sunflower Freedom Project?
HO:     I do feel prepared; but I think; like; in the future that they can      prepare me more for the things that I’ll be facing; like on college      campus.
HI:    Okay.
HI:    So right now; what do you feel prepared to do; as far as maybe      academics; or maybe just as a young woman?
HI:    What kind of things have      they prepared you for so far?
HO:    We write a lot of essays here.
HO:    So; I think that I am capable of      writing an essay for a college; or for a scholarship.
HI:    And what about personally?
HI:    Have they taught you any values; you know;      self-awareness?
HI:    Do you feel like they teach you to be confident; and      to make good relationships with people?
HO:    Okay.

HO:    So; I started at the Freedom Project the summer going into my      freshmen year; and before I came into the Freedom Project; I was      really shy; but now it’s easier for me to talk in front of a group of      people because we have different classes to teach that.

HO:    Also; like the      Freedom Project is a non-profit organization; so when we go on trips;      we don’t sleep in hotels and stuff; we live with host families; and we      camp; we sleep outside and stuff like that.
HO:    So; I think that’s      preparing us.
HI:    Oh; that’s cool; I didn’t know that.
HI:    What is that like; travelling      with a non-profit organization?
HI:    Would you prefer to be able stay in      hotels; or do you like getting to meet new people; and staying with      them; and talking to people; and camping?
HO:    Well; at first; I preferred hotels; because I thought it would be      kinda crazy; and I was afraid at first; because I didn’t know the      people and I was going into their homes.
HO:    But when I got there; it’s      like a family.
HO:    They; like; trust you—people that you don’t even know;      they trust you.
HO:    So when you go into their homes; it’s like friendly:
HO:         it makes you feel like you’re at home.
HO:    And with the camping...
HO:    oh;      my God!
HO:    That was like something so new:
HO:    we literally; we had to go      potty outside.
HO:     That was like something so different to me!
HO:
HI:    Okay.
HI:    Can you tell us some of the history of the Sunflower County      Freedom Project?
HI:    Can you tell us some of the history that you know?
HO:     Okay.
HI:    Like when it was started:
HI:    who started it?
HI:    How long has it been here?
HI:         Who are the founders?
HI:    Stuff like that.
HO:    So; the first original Freedom Project was in Meridian; Mississippi.
HO:         And now; they are starting another Freedom Project there.
HO:    Another      Freedom Project was in Indianola; Mississippi; but it burned.
HO:    It was      like during racial times; it burned.
HO:    A few years ago; students helped      build this building; and it was started by three TFAs.
HO:    When I got here      last year; Mister Nick Allen and Becca Bessy; they were like the      executive producers.
HO:    Missus Shastry and Missus Stevens; they are the newer      ones; and Missus Moses has been here; like; for a long time.
HI:    Okay.
HI:    And do a lot of people come here to visit you guys; or is it      just you guys most of the time?
HO:    A lot of people visit; like a lot of different colleges.
HI:    And what do the colleges usually do when they come?
HO:    They come and they try to learn about the Freedom Project.

HO:    Like most      of the time; if a college group visits; it’s like a college group that      doesn’t know much about us; and they always seem so amazed because of      the way Sunflower County looks like.
HO:    It’s not; like; a pretty place;      but they think that the Freedom Project is a good place; so they’re      like amazed at like how much stuff we can do in communities like this.
HI:    Okay; and what is your favorite part about being here?
HI:    ‘Cause I know      you guys have really long days in school; but then you come here; and      you seem do happy and proud to be a part of it.
HI:    So; what is your      favorite part about being here?
HO:    Honestly; the Freedom Project is like my second family.
HO:    At home; my      parents; they motivate me so much; and it’s like so good knowing that      you have people that want to see you do good.
HO:    And when you come to the      Freedom Project; it’s like a good feeling to know that people wanna      help you.
HO:    And here; they care about you and they push you.
HI:    That’s good.
HI:    Is there a special name for students who attend here?
HI:         Are you guys like the Sunflowers; or have you come up with names for      each other?
HI:    ‘Cause I know the whole school doesn’t come here; so .
HI:    .
HI:    .
HO:    Yeah; we’re called Freedom Fellows.
HI:    Freedom Fellows.
HO:    And we address each other by mister and misses.
HI:    So even the students call each other mister and misses.
HI:    So you would      probably say Miss Brittany; and I would say Miss Breyanna.
HO:    We would say like Miss Hooper; or Miss...
HO:    yeah.
HI:    So; how does that make you feel for someone to give such a title of      respect and you’re so young?
HO:    Actually; at first I was like—I wasn’t not okay with it; but after a      while; it grows onto you; and it makes you feel like you’re      professional.
HI:    And what do you want to do when you grow up?
HI:    Because I’m imagining      that them saying; you know; Miss Hooper; makes you feel respected and      it gives you kind of—
HO:    It gives you authority.
HI:    Exactly!
HI:    So do you know what you want to do already when you get      older?
HO:    Yeah; I wanna be a psychologist.
HI:    You wanna be a psychologist.
HI:    So; they’re gonna call you Doctor Hooper.
HI:         Do you feel that you already can see yourself being a doctor because      you’re so used to hearing them respect you here?
HO:    I can.
HO:    It grows on you.
HI:    And what does that mean for you as a black woman to have someone;      your peers and adults; call you Miss Hooper?
HO:    It makes me feel like a lot of people look up to me; like I actually      feel respected.
HO:    Even the older students; they address us as mister and      missus; and I feel respected by everyone.
HI:    That’s a good feeling.
HI:    How does that make you feel to have even older      students call you respect?
HI:    Like do you guys ever have trouble with the      older students not wanting to call you Miss Hooper?
HO:    No; not actually.
HO:    I am considered an older student; ‘cause I’m in      high school.
HO:    But still; the seniors and the juniors; it makes me feel      like they look up to me too.
HI:    That’s good.
HI:    And what is high school like here?
HI:    ‘Cause I know you go      to high school in Drew?
HI:    What is high school like?
HO:    It’s wild.
HO:    Oh; my God; it’s wild.
HO:    So; it’s like a town thing; I would      say:
HO:    Sunflower and Drew and Ruleville; they’re like against each      other.
HO:    And all of us are stuck in this school; I promise you; they      fight like almost every day.
HO:    They have police officers to check      everybody in school; and they’ve actually found guns and knives and      everything like that on people.
HO:    We—
HI:    Why do you think the violence is so bad between three cities?
HO:    I’m not sure why.
HO:    It started over something crazy; it started over a      song dissing a town; and it went from there; which is kinda crazy.
HO:    I      promise you; I always tell them; I don’t think there is anything to      fight about; because the towns are alike.
HO:    Like both of us have      nothing; and I tell them; if they keep on doing these things we’ll      stay without having anything.
HI:    Mm-hm; and how long ago was that song released?
HO:    Maybe...
HO:    it was over the summer; I think.
HI:    So; it was recently that there’s been a fight.
HO:    Mm-hm; and it’s been going on since last year.
HI:    Since last year.
HO:    It was the summer of last year.
HI:    Has anybody close to you been hurt in the violence?
HO:    Not close to me; but recently—it was like two weeks ago; after a      game; a boy from Drew; he got jumped and he got beat so bad; like he      was just messed up.
HI:    You spoke about earlier feeling safer in where you previously came      from.
HI:    Do you think that; by the time you’re a high school senior;      it’ll be safer here?
HO:    If things keep going the way they are going; no; I don’t think it      will be safe.
HI:    Now; you; being a young woman; how do you think you guys can improve      what’s going on between the three cities?
HI:    Like what are some practical      ways right now that you guys can fix what’s going on?
HO:    Well; the things that I’ve tried.
HO:    And honestly I think they can stop      them; just tell them how foolish it is.
HO:    And I honestly think that they      won’t stop until someone that they really care about gets hurt.
HO:    That’s      how I feel about it.
HI:    Okay.

HI:    Now; if you guys were given a whole lot of money—like; say      somebody came down here with like a hundred thousand dollar check; and      was like; we wanna give this to the Freedom Fellows that are here.
HI:         What improvements would you make to; I guess; the city of Sunflower      and also to this building and your project?
HI:    Like what type of things      would you do here?
HO:    Honestly; the Freedom Project has a lot of damage; like; everywhere;      like our roof that leaks and stuff like that; so I would honestly fix      that first.
HO:    And then I would fix our garden; like fix stuff that’ll      make the Freedom Project more productive; and maybe more students will      try to come; and then go on to help the community.
HI:    So; things like maybe computers and maybe more textbooks.
HI:    What are      some of the things you wish you had here?
HO:    Here...
HO:    more books; honestly.
HO:    Because our library is nice; but I      think we should have more books.
HI:    More books.
HO:    Yeah.
HI:    And what else as far as; you know; would you paint?
HI:    Like would you      put more murals up?
HI:    Because outside when we were coming; we were so      shocked.
HI:    Like we had to stop; and we were like; oh; my God that’s so      beautiful!
HI:    We like stopped the van in the middle of the street so we      could take a picture.
HI:    So; I mean; your murals are beautiful.
HI:    So; would      you probably put more murals up in here and around a building?
HO:    Yeah.
HO:    Have you noticed in the top; in the ceiling?
HI:    In the other room:
HI:    it’s a beautiful mural.
HO:    Yeah.
HI:    I was in the classroom like this.
HI:     Like I was trying to      read; we were talking about the book; and I’m looking up at the      ceiling; like; wow; this is beautiful.
HI:    Artwork is a very big part of      what you guys have placed forth here.
HI:    Do you think artwork is a great      way of advertising or maybe showing about the Project?
HO:    Actually; it is.
HO:    A lot of people that come to the Freedom Project are      artists; and we do have an art class.
HO:    Most of the time; the Freedom      Project has a poster around; and it’s gonna be filled with art.
HO:    And I      think that’s what draws people like my age attention; creativity.
HI:    That’s very interesting.
HI:    And what do you tell people about the      Freedom Project?
HI:    Because I didn’t know nothing about it.
HI:    So say; for      example; a random person in the street came up to you and was like;      Breyanna; tell me about the Freedom Project.
HI:    What would you say?
HO:    So; it’s school.
HO:    A lot of people would not come to the Freedom      Project; because they push us; they give us extra work.
HO:    Like we have      homework at school; but at the Freedom Project; we have work; too.
HO:    And      they think it’s crazy for us to do all this work.
HO:    At school; I try to      explain to them that it’s not just the way they make it seem.
HO:    They      don’t like the time that we come here; leave; and they think it’s like      uncalled for and stuff.
HI:    If not just high school students; if an adult asked you what you do      here; how would you describe the Freedom Project?
HO:    I would tell them that it’s a good place.
HO:    I would tell them that;      since I came to the Freedom Project; I’ve grown in a lot of different      things.
HO:    Like; I’ve never been a C student; but at a point in time; I      was making low B’s.
HO:    But since I’ve started doing the Freedom project;      I’ve got my grades back up to high A’s; but the reason I was making      the low B’s was because after school; had nothing to do.
HO:    I would just      do enough to get by.
HO:    But here; you actually have time to do stuff; and      they will not let you slack:
HO:    they keep you on top of your game.
HI:    Now; it sounds like there are just so amazing things going on here.
HI:         Do you guys fundraise to help keep the school up?
HO:    Mm-hm.
HI:    What ways do you guys fundraise?
HO:    So; going to the Freedom Project you have to pay a tuition.
HO:    And      instead of your parents paying the entire thing; you can sell donuts.
HI:    How much; if you don’t mind me asking; is the tuition to come here?
HO:    One hundred fifty.
HI:    Is that for the year; or is that for...
HI:    ?
HO:    It depends.
HO:    So; we have a summer school program and a year-round      program.
HO:    Both of them are a hundred and fifty.
HI:    Okay.
HI:    And do you think if there was more money; like if more students      in your community could afford to pay the tuition; do you think more      students would come?
HI:    Or are students only coming because they don’t      wanna do the work?
HO:    They won’t come ‘cause they don’t wanna do the work.
HI:    But do you think fundraising would help if more students could afford      the one-fifty?
HO:    It would:
HO:    it does help a lot.
HO:    All you have to do is; I think; sell      like fifty boxes and that’s it.
HI:    And be able to come.
HI:    Trying to think of what else I can ask.
HI:    You      know; you’ve answered everything so well; but I feel like it’s such an      amazing program here that a lot of people don’t know about.
HI:    ‘Cause I      had no idea what I was coming up to.
HO:    So; this is your first time coming here?
HI:    Yeah; this is my first time in Mississippi.
HI:    It’s my first time being      here; too; so you guys are doing like amazing stuff here.
HI:    So; just      tell me; what’s that like; living in Mississippi?
HI:    Like what can you      possibly do here?
HO:    Actually; in Mississippi?
HO:    Nothing.
HO:    Nothing; but shop.
HO:    I find shopping      fun; ‘cause that’s the only thing in Mississippi.
HO:    But if you go to;      like; Tennessee or places like that; that’s when you can have fun.
HI:    So; what do you guys do for fun?
HI:    Like you’re on a weekend:
HI:    I know you      come here on Saturdays; but you have down time.
HI:    What do you?
HO:    Activities.
HO:    Skating rink; bowling alley; moving theaters; stuff like      that.
HI:    Okay; and what else—you spoke about going to college in Mississippi.
HI:         Are you looking at any schools outside of Mississippi?
HI:    We talked about      Spelman:
HI:    are you thinking about going up north; or do you wanna stay      in the South?
HI:    Are you trying to go to like the west coast; or...
HI:    ?
HO:    Actually; I’m not deciding.
HO:    But if I had the choice to go to a      college in Mississippi; I think it would be Ole Miss.
HO:    I like the      environment; and everyone is; like; so friendly.
HO:    And we took classes      there this summer:
HO:    like public speaking; and we took art classes; we      took film classes.
HO:    And I like the environment.
HI:    So; you guys actually went to Ole Miss and got to take classes.
HI:    What      was that like; being on Ole Miss’s campus and being able to take      classes?
HO:    It was different; I would say.
HO:    It’s not like down here; and; like; we      got a chance to interact with a lot of college students.
HI:    And did the college students have any advice for you guys as to how      to get into college or what to do for college life?
HI:    Like what did they      tell you?
HO:    They told us to read and write a lot; ‘cause there’s a lot in      college.
HI:    That’s very true.
HI:     It’s a lot of reading and writing; and      you read and write till your hands hurt.
HI:    It’s not so many much exams      as before.
HI:    Like if you’re in a major where there’s a lot of science or      math; then you have a lot of exams.
HI:    But I’m a history major; and I      read and write all the time:
HI:    that’s all I do is read and write.
HI:    That’s      it.
HI:    So; I mean; you’re gonna be in psychology; so you’re gonna have      exams.
HI:    But you also will read and write because you get to write      papers:
HI:    you know; so that’ll be cool for you; too.
HI:    Well; I’m so      thankful that; you know especially us coming from a big school; we get      the chance to come down here and see what amazing things you guys are      doing.
HI:    Because I would love to bring this information back to my      school; and be able to tell them what you guys are doing here.
HI:    So what      I wanna do; I just wanna wrap up and; first of all; tell you thank you      again for being here; and working so hard; and it will pay off.
HI:    And      I’m gonna keep in touch with you; and I hope if you need anything; you      definitely reach out to us at the Samuel Proctor Oral History Program;      or even just me individually.
HI:    So; just once again; today is September      21; 2013.
HI:    I’m sitting here with Breyanna Hooper; and we just wrapped      up our interview here at the Sunflower County Freedom Project.
HI:    Thank      you; Breyanna.
HO:    You’re welcome.
HI:    No problem; sweetheart.
